scope.start: 59b: the Mishnayot of lending a garment and of three women sharing one garment or bench, and Rav's qualification (60a opens mid-statement)
scope.end: 60b: the baraita of *keitzad tolot zo b'zo*, which runs into 61a

sections.title: Lending a Garment to a Gentile or a Niddah
sections.gist: The Mishnah lets a woman blame a stain on the gentile or menstruating woman who borrowed her garment, and the Gemara asks how plausible a bleeder that borrower must be.

children.title: Mishnah: She Attributes the Stain to the Borrower
children.gist: A stain found after a gentile woman or a *niddah* wore the garment is attributed to her, because she loses nothing by it.

bullets.text: Mishnah: she lent her garment to a gentile woman or to a menstruating woman; after it was returned she wore it and found a blood stain — she attributes the stain to the borrower.
The attribution costs nobody anything: the *niddah* is already impure, and the gentile woman's status is not governed by these laws.
No showing is required that the stain is *more likely* the borrower's; since *kesamim* are rabbinic, the availability of a party who does not lose is itself enough.

children.title: Rav: The Gentile Must Already Have Seen Blood
children.gist: Rav restricts the Mishnah to a gentile woman who has menstruated; Rav Sheshet attacks him from a baraita, and Rava resolves it by showing R. Meir is the lenient voice.

bullets.text: Rav: the Mishnah speaks of a gentile woman who is of age and has already experienced a flow of menstrual blood.
His inference: the gentile woman of the Mishnah is *dumya deniddah* — like the *niddah* listed beside her, one who actually sees blood.

Rav Sheshet: Rav said this while dozing. A baraita permits attributing the stain to a gentile woman without qualification, and even R. Meir requires only that she be *re'uyah lirot*, fit to see blood — not that she ever bled.
Rava: how can you read R. Meir as the stringent one? R. Meir comes to be lenient.

Proof: a second baraita has the first *tanna* say she may *not* attribute the stain to a gentile woman at all, while R. Meir says she may. So the first *tanna* permits it only where she once bled (as Rav said), and R. Meir permits it wherever she is of an age to bleed.

The dispute shows that *tliyah* needs plausibility as well as costlessness: a stain cannot be pinned on someone for whom bleeding is absurd — the question is only how much of a track record is needed.

chart.caption: The two baraitot on attributing a stain to a gentile woman, as Rava reads them
rows: "She attributes the stain to the gentile woman"
"She may not attribute the stain to a gentile woman"
Only a gentile who once actually experienced a flow — Rav's ruling
"Only a gentile woman fit to see menstrual blood"
"She may attribute the stain to her"
Old enough to bleed, even if she never has — the lenient view

sections.title: Three Women, One Garment or One Bench
sections.gist: Where the candidates are equal, attribution collapses and all three are impure — unless the bench itself is not susceptible to impurity, in which case R. Nechemia purifies them.

bullets.text: Mishnah: three women wore one garment in turn, or sat one after another on one bench; it was examined and clean before the first, and a stain was found after the third — all the women are impure.

When no woman is a likelier source than the others, attribution to any one of them at the others' expense cannot be justified, so no one is spared — like two roads with a corpse under one, where each traveler alone would be pure but both together cannot be.
Mishnah: if they sat on a stone bench or on the *itzteva* of a bathhouse — the one because it is stone, the other because it is attached to the floor — R. Nechemia declares them pure.
R. Nechemia's principle: *kol davar she'eino mekabel tumah eino mekabel ketamim* — the decree of impurity for stains was limited to items susceptible to ritual impurity.

Tosafos: this shows the whole framework of *kesamim* was built inside *tumah v'taharah*. The woman's status is derived from the object's; if the object cannot be declared impure, the chain never reaches her.
Hence the practical weight today of whether plastic, polyester and nylon are *mekabel tumah* — even only rabbinically — for a stain found on them.

sections.title: Unequal Loss: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel vs. Rabbi
sections.gist: A baraita on lending to a *shomeret yom* or a woman counting seven clean days sets up the central dispute: may a stain be attributed to someone who loses, but loses less?

children.title: The Baraita: Shomeret Yom and Soferet Shiv'ah
children.gist: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel attributes the stain to the borrower who stands to lose less; Rabbi refuses, so both women are ruined.

bullets.text: Baraita: the lender may attribute the stain to a borrower who is a *shomeret yom keneged yom* on her second day — her womb is regarded as open and bleeding is likely.

Likewise if she lent it to a woman counting seven clean days who had not yet immersed and would now have to count seven again: the lender's status is fixed and the borrower's is ruined — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: she may not attribute the stain to either of these women; therefore both statuses are ruined and both women are impure.

The loss is sharply unequal — the borrower forfeits one watch-day or restarts a count while still impure, whereas the lender would become a *niddah* for seven days. For Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that asymmetry licenses attribution; for Rabbi any real loss bars it.

Attributes — the borrower recounts her seven days

No attribution — both women are impure

children.title: Where Both Agree: Attribution That Costs Nothing
children.gist: Three borrowers whose status attribution cannot harm — and everyone permits attributing the stain to them.

bullets.text: Both agree she may attribute the stain to a *shomeret yom* on her first day, since she is impure that day in any case and can still purify herself the next day.
Both agree where the borrower was a woman after childbirth observing her days of *dam tohor*, whose blood does not affect her status.
Both agree about a virgin after her first intercourse, whose blood is presumed hymenal and pure.
Wherever attribution is costless everyone attributes freely; the dispute is confined to cases of genuine but asymmetric loss.

children.title: Why the Two "Therefore" Clauses
children.gist: The Gemara justifies the baraita's doubled *lefikach*: Rabbi's clause rules out pinning the stain on whoever happened to be wearing the garment.

bullets.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's "therefore" clause adds nothing; it was taught only for the sake of the parallel "therefore" in Rabbi's statement.
Rabbi's "therefore" is needed lest one say that only the woman wearing the garment when the stain was found is ruined, while the other is spared because the garment was not with her. Both are impure.

sections.title: Two Paths: Applying the Dispute to Corpse Impurity
sections.gist: Rav Chisda transfers the dispute to an impure and a pure man who walked two paths, one impure from a buried corpse; Rav Adda resists the analogy.

children.title: Rav Chisda: The Same Dispute
children.gist: May the impure path be assigned to the man who is already impure, sparing the pure man? Rav Chisda says this is exactly Rabbi against Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

bullets.text: Rav Chisda: an impure man and a pure man walked two paths, one pure and one impure from a buried corpse, neither recalls which he took, and afterwards they handled *terumah* or consecrated food — we have arrived at the dispute of Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
For Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, assume the already-impure man walked the impure path and the other remains pure; Rabbi holds there is no such assumption, since the pure man may equally have walked it.

Tosafot: the case must be one where the impure man is already some days into his purification, so that adding corpse impurity genuinely sets him back — but not necessarily one who has nearly finished, since Rabbi objects even to a single day's loss.

children.title: Rav Adda's Objection and Rav Chisda's Answer
children.gist: Rav Adda says Rabbi objected only where the two parties are alike; Rav Chisda answers that the *shomeret yom* is not pure either.

bullets.text: Rav Adda objects: perhaps Rabbi ruled that way only with the *shomeret yom*, who can immerse at any time, so both women are alike in having a presumption of purity — but here, what practical difference does it make to a man who is already impure?
Rav Chisda's answer: the *shomeret yom* is not fully pure either — *sof sof tevilah ba'aya*, she still needs immersion — and Rabbi nonetheless refused the attribution; so the cases are comparable.

The two amora'im are really arguing about what drives Rabbi: an absolute refusal to impose any incremental loss, or a narrower rule that applies only where the parties are essentially equivalent in status.

children.title: R. Yosi son of R. Chanina: A Pure Man and a Doubtfully Impure One
children.gist: Where the other man is impure only by doubt, all agree the impure path is assigned to him — a statement that fits Rav Adda rather than Rav Chisda.

bullets.text: R. Yosi son of R. Chanina: where one man is pure and the other impure by doubt and they walked the two paths, one attributes the impure path to the doubtfully impure man and the pure path to the pure man — and everyone agrees, Rabbi included.
The Gemara observes that this statement accords with Rav Adda's objection and not with Rav Chisda's suggestion.
The *talui* must treat himself as impure in any event, so the attribution costs him nothing — which assumes the first day; if it would add days of impurity, the dispute would return.

sections.title: Attributing a Stain to a Woman Who Has a Stain
sections.gist: May a *ketem* be blamed on a woman whose own impurity rests only on a *ketem*? A dilemma, a self-contradictory baraita, and four attempts to settle it.

children.title: R. Yochanan's Dilemma to R. Yehuda bar Livai
children.gist: The question is only for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; the answer given is that a stain may not be attributed to a woman impure from a stain.

bullets.text: R. Yochanan asked R. Yehuda bar Livai: may a blood stain be attributed to a woman who is impure only because she found a blood stain of her own?
He brackets Rabbi's view: if there, with a *shomeret yom* who sees a discharge from her body, Rabbi will not attribute, then here, where her impurity came from a source outside her body, surely not.
So the dilemma is for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: does he permit attribution only to a woman who actually bled from her body, or does a woman with a mere stain make no difference?
R. Yehuda bar Livai: she may not attribute it to her, and both women are impure — because that woman's own stain may itself have come from an external cause.

children.title: The Baraita That Contradicts Itself, and Three Resolutions
children.gist: One clause forbids attributing a stain to a stained woman and the next permits it; the Gemara splits them between the two tanna'im, between first and second day, or between retroactive and future status.

bullets.text: Baraita brought against him: one may not attribute a stain to a woman impure from a previous stain — yet if she lent her garment to a gentile woman, or to a woman observing days of impurity from a stain, she may attribute it to her. The baraita contradicts itself.
R. Yochanan's resolution: the first clause follows Rabbi and the latter clause follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

Others say: both clauses are Rabbi. The permissive clause is her first day, when she is impure anyway and loses nothing; the restrictive clause is her second day, when she is merely awaiting immersion and attribution would cost her an extra day.

Rav Ashi: both clauses are Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — *kan lemapre'a kan lehaba*. The permissive clause concerns rendering her retroactively impure for pure items she had already touched, which costs her nothing; the restrictive clause concerns her status going forward, which would ruin her count.

The shiur reads *lemapre'a* and *lehaba* as a rule about the moment of ruling: a stain already found is available as a basis for attribution, while one discovered only later cannot reopen a determination already made — halachic status is fixed formally, not merely evidentially.

children.title: Ravina Rereads the Permissive Clause
children.gist: Since every resolution still has Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permitting stain-on-stain attribution, Ravina rereads the baraita so that it never permits it.

bullets.text: The objection remains: on all these readings Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel does allow attributing a stain to a woman who had seen a stain, against R. Yehuda bar Livai's answer.

Ravina: the latter clause means that if she lent her garment to a gentile woman, then as regards defining *the lender* as one who saw a stain, she may attribute her stain to the gentile — nothing is learned about attributing to a woman with a stain.

But the *tanna* also says "or to a woman observing days of impurity from a stain"? Ravina rereads that too: or to a woman after childbirth observing her days of *dam tohor* — and the lender remains pure.
The rereading leaves *ein tolin ketem beketem* intact: in each permitted case there is an independent feature — gentile status or *dam tohor* — that justifies the attribution.

sections.title: R. Nechemia's Rule Examined and Ruled Upon
sections.gist: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah's stone bench: R. Nechemia's scriptural source, how far "not susceptible" reaches, and whether the *halakha* follows him.

returns_to.note: Takes up R. Nechemia's ruling in the Mishnah of the stone and bathhouse benches

children.title: Rav Mattana: "And Clean She Shall Sit Upon the Ground"
children.gist: R. Nechemia's rule is derived from Yeshayahu's verse about sitting on the ground.

bullets.text: Rav Mattana: R. Nechemia's reason is the verse "and clean she shall sit upon the ground" (Yeshayahu 3:26) — once she sits on the ground, which is not susceptible to impurity, she is clean.

children.title: The Exterior of an Earthenware Vessel
children.gist: Rav Huna in R. Chanina's name extends the rule to a surface that cannot contract impurity even though the vessel can, and the Gemara explains why this needed saying.

bullets.text: Rav Huna said R. Chanina: R. Nechemia would declare her pure even for a stain on the exterior of an earthenware vessel, since such a vessel contracts impurity only through its inner airspace.
Isn't that obvious? It is needed lest one say the Sages decreed impurity on the outside because of its resemblance to the inside; the Gemara teaches that no such decree was made.
The test is therefore whether *this surface* is susceptible, not whether the object in general belongs to a susceptible category.

children.title: Abaye: Rags Smaller Than Three by Three
children.gist: A rag too small to serve anyone is not susceptible, so a stain on it does not implicate the woman.

bullets.text: Abaye: R. Nechemia would declare her pure for stains seen on small rags lacking three fingerbreadths by three, since such rags are fit for use neither by the poor nor by the wealthy.

children.title: Halakha Like R. Nechemia, and Rav Nachman's Challenge
children.gist: Rav rules like R. Nechemia; Rav Nachman cites cases where the Sages declared women impure, and the answer is that the Sages themselves are divided.

bullets.text: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana taught in Rav's name: the *halakha* follows R. Nechemia.
Rav Nachman objected: my father teaches a baraita in which such an incident came before the Sages and they declared both women impure — and you say the *halakha* follows R. Nechemia?

The baraita: two women grinding at a hand mill — blood beneath the inner woman, both are impure, since the outer one pushes in toward the mill; beneath the outer woman, she is impure and the inner one pure; found between them, both are impure.

The same baraita: blood was found on the rim of a bathtub, and a stain on an olive leaf while the women were kindling the oven; the case came before the Sages and they declared both impure — though an olive leaf is not susceptible to impurity.

Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana answers: it is a dispute among *tanna'im* — another baraita has R. Yaakov declaring her impure and R. Nechemia declaring her pure, with the Sages ruling in accordance with R. Nechemia.
Three structural leniencies now stand in the law of stains: a minimum size of a *geris*, an object that is *mekabel tumah*, and undyed garments only.
The same three conditions govern *tum'at nega'im*, raising the question whether the criteria of *kesamim* were reasoned out practically or shaped by a formal analogy to the laws of *tzara'at*.

sections.title: Three Women Sleeping in One Bed
sections.gist: A new Mishnah: blood beneath one of three sleepers makes all impure unless one identifies herself as the source, and the Gemara asks how quickly she must examine herself.

children.title: The Mishnah's Four Rulings
children.gist: All three are impure; one who examines herself and finds she is menstruating clears the others; otherwise they attribute the blood to one another, and if none is fit to bleed all are impure.

bullets.text: Mishnah: three women were sleeping in one bed and blood was discovered beneath one of them — all of them are impure.
If when the blood was discovered one of them examined herself and found she was impure from menstruation, she is impure and the other two are pure.
If none examined themselves, or all examined and were pure, they attribute the blood to one another — a woman unfit to menstruate attributes it to those who are fit.
If all three were unfit to see blood, they are regarded as though they were fit and all three are impure, since the blood must have come from one of them.
All are impure at the outset because sleepers are presumed to shift about, so the stain's position beneath one woman does not identify her as its source.

children.title: Rav: Only an Examination Within Shiur Veset Clears the Others
children.gist: The self-examination exempts the other two only if it was made within the brief span for the onset of menses.

bullets.text: Rav Yehuda said Rav: the other two women are cleared only where she examined herself within *shiur veset*, the brief period needed for the onset of menstruation.
If she examined herself later, she is impure but the others are impure as well, out of doubt — she may have become a *niddah* only after the blood was found.
Rav holds in accordance with bar Padda.

children.title: Bar Padda's Three Periods
children.gist: Bar Padda ties the status of items a woman handled to the offering her husband would owe: sin offering and burning, provisional guilt offering and suspension, or exemption and purity.

bullets.text: Bar Padda: there are three periods for a woman who finds blood after intercourse — within *shiur veset*; the time needed to get out of bed and wash; and anything longer.
Any period in which her husband would be liable for a *chatat* is one in which, had she instead been handling pure food and then found blood, the items she touched are impure and burned.
Where her husband would bring an *asham talui*, the items she handled are suspended — neither burned nor eaten.
Where he is exempt from any offering, the items she handled remain pure.
Rashi notes the tension with the tractate's opening, where a woman's impurity is presumed retroactively *me'et le'et*; the Gemara does not press it here.

children.title: R. Oshaya: The Offering and the Taharot Come Apart
children.gist: R. Oshaya severs the parallel — only intercourse physically held the blood back — and two parables illustrate his reasoning.

bullets.text: R. Oshaya: there is no link between the husband's offering and the status of the items; even where he is liable for a *chatat*, the pure items she touched are only suspended.

His reasoning: granted that in intercourse the male organ prevented the blood from emerging, so it was clearly there beforehand — but while she was preparing food in purity, what was holding the blood back?

R. Yirmeya's parable for R. Oshaya's view: a child walking with an old man keeps to his pace on the road, but once they enter the city the child hastens ahead — so blood held back during intercourse comes at once when it ends.
Abaye's parable: a finger in the eye holds the tears back; the moment it is removed the tears hasten to come.
Hence the standards diverge: absent such a mechanism we assume the blood emerged only when it was found, so an examination outside the context of intercourse cannot establish an earlier status.

children.title: Keitzad Tolot Zo B'Zo: The Baraita's Four Pairs
children.gist: A baraita spells out the differential attributions — pregnant, nursing, old and pre-menarche women blame the blood on the woman more likely to bleed — and closes with the case where both are alike.

bullets.text: Baraita: how do they attribute the blood to one another? If one woman is pregnant and the other is not, the pregnant one attributes the blood to the woman who is not pregnant.
If one is nursing and the other is not, the nursing woman attributes the blood to the one who is not nursing.
If one is old and no longer bleeds regularly and the other is not old, the old woman attributes the blood to the one who is not old.
If one is a virgin — here, one who has not yet experienced bleeding — and the other is not, the virgin attributes the blood to the one who has already bled.
If both are pregnant, both nursing, both old or both virgins, this is the Mishnah's case: though unfit to see blood, they are regarded as though they were fit.

chart.caption: The baraita's differential attributions among women sharing a bed
rows: The pregnant woman attributes to the one who is not
The nursing woman attributes to the one who is not
The old woman attributes to the one who is not
The virgin attributes to the one who has bled
Treated as though fit to see — all impure

children.continues: Continues on 61a: they are regarded as fit and all three are impure; then the Mishnah of three women in a bed set against a wall.

judgment_calls: Rav Chisda's two-paths discussion (s9) could have been nested as a child of the Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel–Rabbi dispute (s5), since the Gemara presents it as an application of that dispute; made top-level because it develops its own three-step argument (Rav Chisda, Rav Adda, R. Yosi son of R. Chanina) in a different body of law.

The *ketem b'ketem* discussion (s13) is likewise framed as a question within the Rabbi / Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dispute, but was given top-level status because it runs through a dilemma, a self-contradictory baraita and four resolutions.

R. Nechemia's Gemara (s17) was left where it falls on 60b with a returns_to link to the Mishnah (s4), rather than merged into the Mishnah section; the shiur's Tosafos framing of the principle was kept with the Mishnah, where the lecture placed it.

Bar Padda and R. Oshaya (s25–s26) could stand as an independent sugya on retroactive impurity; kept as children of the three-women Mishnah because the Gemara brings them only to ground Rav's *shiur veset* condition.

The shiur's summary of the three leniencies of *kesamim* and their parallel to *nega'im* has no counterpart in the Gemara text; it was folded into s21 as detail-3 shiur bullets rather than given its own section.
coverage_notes: The Mishnayot at 59b.19–21 are included in scope because 60a opens in the middle of the Gemara's discussion of them, and the shiur treats them.
The essay credits the resolution of the two gentile-woman baraitot to 'Rav Papa'; the text has Rava. Followed the text.

The essay credits the rereading of the baraita's permissive clause to Abaye ('nochrit ba'alat ketem'); the text has Ravina, and his reading makes the *lender* the one who saw a stain, with the second case reread as a woman observing *dam tohor*. Followed the text.

The essay explains Rav Ashi's *kan lemapre'a kan lehaba* via Tosafos (a stain already found vs. one discovered after the ruling); the Sefaria text explains it as retroactive impurity for items she already touched vs. her status going forward. Followed the text and kept the shiur's reading as a shiur bullet.

The essay speaks of 'Rabbi Yoshia's principle' as the basis for bar Padda's ruling; in the text it is R. Oshaya who disputes bar Padda, and the parables of R. Yirmeya and Abaye are given in explanation of R. Oshaya's opinion. Followed the text.
The essay presents R. Yosi son of R. Chanina's ruling only as unanimous; the text adds that it accords with Rav Adda's objection and not with Rav Chisda's suggestion. Included from the text.
The essay describes Rav Adda's objection as claiming the *shomeret yom* is nearly pure; the text has him add that the already-impure man loses nothing at all by the attribution. Followed the text.
